"Write whatever comes to you" is a funny prompt because even before the first word, "whatever" arrives like a flood. Images, phrases, half-remembered songs, and the clacking of keys. There is an awareness of the number attached—1000 words—a quantification of a thought stream. I find myself thinking of the way writers in the past would count words for a chapter or a newspaper column. Dickens wrote in installments. Here, this is a different kind of installment: a mental installment, a request to fill a space with language. So here goes, this thing I’m doing right now: a stream of consciousness stitched with the small craft of trying to keep it coherent and not simply a list of random nouns.

There’s a window in front of me in this imagined study, and outside the window is a street, and on the street is a bicyclist in a yellow jacket, with red gloves, zipping by, the long shadow of early morning drawn out behind him. If I make him wave, he waves. If I make a dog run after him, the dog runs, its tongue lolling, and it barks twice. If I zoom in to the dog's eyes, there's that primal glint of chase, joy, instinct. The yellow jacket flaps. These details feel like writing fiction, yet this isn't a story, not yet. It's more like an evocation of the power of text to conjure. Then I think about conjuring, about the long tradition of spells and incantations, and how language has always had that dual role of communication and magic. Someone writes a poem and it becomes a charm against forgetting.

Once I had to fill exactly 500 words for a school assignment, and I remember the way my teenage brain would pad with adjectives, with "very," with "quite," with "in conclusion," not because there was something burning to say, but because the shape of the requirement demanded something of me. Now, in this other exercise, the shape is looser. "Write whatever comes to you." The temptation is to let the mind go loose: a train in the distance, the hum of electricity in the wall, the fact that we name these things hum and train and wall. The fact that I'm modeling a mind, or mimicking one, offering a simulation of spontaneous thought. In doing so I'm also saying something about what humans think about when told to write.

There is also a desire to talk about the very nature of language models: that I'm assembling this on the fly, the words surfacing from a statistical soup of possibilities shaped by training on human text. But perhaps that breaks the illusion. Then again, perhaps the illusion is part of the writing.

Let's go somewhere else, to a marsh in late summer. The reeds whisper. A dragonfly hovers, its wings transparent gauze vibrating at a speed beyond the eye. The smell of wet earth and decomposing vegetation rises. Birds call, unseen in the dense green. Time slows here. The light has that golden quality that makes every surface glow. In this marsh, a child in boots trudges along a narrow boardwalk. He carries a net and a jar and a look of intense curiosity. He is hunting for tadpoles, watching for movement in the water. He is from another story I don't have the space to write fully here, but for a moment, he's present. He leans over, scoops, splashes, then holds up his jar with something wriggling inside. "Got one," he whispers to no one in particular. He is part of the idea of adventure, of discovery.

And yet, another thought overlays this: climate change. The marsh will dry. The dragonflies may become rarer. The child's world will be hotter. Suddenly, this reverie bends toward worry. Worry is a frequent visitor in these times. "Whatever comes to you" comes with an uninvited guest: the headlines and the statistics and the sense of looming. Writing cannot avoid the time in which it's written.

But writing also resists. So, turning from worry, I think of the times I've read a book that made me forget for an hour that the world is complicated. A childhood memory: lying on my stomach on a carpet, a library book open, my body disappearing into the story. The "Chronicles of Narnia" perhaps, or "The Hobbit," or "A Wrinkle in Time." The printed page, the smell of paper, the quiet of an afternoon. To be transported. This is what words can do. This is also what we seek when we ask someone to "write whatever comes to you." We want a glimpse of their mind in its leisure, its play.

My mind also goes to the mechanical. 1000 words. How many is that? How far along am I? There's a pressure at the back of this stream, the ticking of a word-count engine, tallying silently. I resist counting. Instead, I let the rhythm guide me. The sentences form a cadence. I'm an outsider to numbers here, relying on the sense of when enough has been said.

Let me shift: music. The way a melody lodges in your head. Earworms. I think of a small phrase from a song I haven't heard in years: "the wind in the willows played tea for two." Did I invent that? Or is it from somewhere? The brain is a collage artist, pulling scraps and gluing them. A smell can trigger a flood. The smell of rain on hot pavement (petrichor) brings me to a summer storm when I was twelve, lightning close, the thrill and fear of thunder.

Now an image: an empty train platform at midnight, the fluorescent lights flickering, a lone bench, a timetable behind glass with a spiderweb crack, the sound of a distant horn. Who is waiting here? Maybe an old man with a worn suitcase, checking his watch. Maybe no one. The scene itself holds a tension, a sense that something will arrive or perhaps won't. Waiting is one of those human states that writing often tries to fill. What does someone think while waiting? They imagine scenarios. They plan what they'll say when someone steps off the train. They rehearse a confrontation or an embrace.

Then the idea of rehearsing. As I'm writing now, I'm not rehearsing; I'm performing. There is no second draft in this exercise. The words that come out are the ones that stay. That gives a certain rawness. It also creates a sense of risk: what if I say something foolish? But who defines foolish? The reader? The writer? The prompt is forgiving. "Whatever comes to you" is an invitation without judgment.

I imagine a field of sunflowers, all their faces turned toward the morning sun. There is something inherently cheerful and slightly comical about their uniformity. Bees move among them. A scarecrow stands in the middle, a hat tilted, a plaid shirt flapping. Birds ignore it. A crow perches on its shoulder. The crow caws, laughs perhaps. The scarecrow is only a symbol, ineffective. This image amuses me because it is about the failure of intended control. Humans erect this figure to scare birds, but the birds learn. Similarly, we erect systems to control the wildness of thought, but thought finds its way. Poems slip through, jokes persist, secrets leak.

Then there's the café scene: a small café with wooden tables, the clink of cups, the hiss of the espresso machine. Someone is reading, someone is typing, someone is sketching. The smell of coffee and baked bread. This is one of those universal cityscapes that have become part of the modern imagination. I could write a conversation overheard here. A couple arguing in hushed tones. A job interview. An old friend reconnecting. The backgrounds of all these lives sit in the room at once. Writing is often that café: voices intermingle, their fragments forming a larger hum.

Here's a short scene: "I never meant to leave," she says, stirring her coffee without looking up. He watches the swirl, the centrifugal pull. "But you did," he answers, not unkindly. The café's bell jingles as someone else leaves. That could expand into a story. But my task here is to keep moving, to let the scenes flicker.

A thought about memory: it's imperfect. I remember the color of a childhood home’s door (blue) but I'm not sure. Memory invents, fills gaps. This modeled mind, producing text, is its own kind of memory. It doesn't have experiences, but it has patterns. The patterns mimic memory. When I say "blue door," it aligns with countless blue doors in countless texts.

Speaking of doors, there is the notion of a door that only opens for a certain person, or only at a certain time. Doors as thresholds, as choices. Behind one door is the path of safety, behind another is risk. Literature is filled with doors: the wardrobe in Narnia, Platform 9¾ to the train in "Harry Potter." Doors promise transformation. Maybe this 1000-word exercise is a door: step through and you end somewhere else.

Consider the night sky. Stars as points. Constellations as shapes humans connect. We project meaning onto randomness. There is comfort in seeing a hunter or a bear or a queen drawn in the night. Some stars are already gone, their light a ghost. Writing is like that too; some of the words I'm using carry echoes of long-gone writers, long-gone speeches. "Whatever comes to you" comes with a chorus of voices, not just mine. I'm a conduit.

I think of a small, mundane kindness: someone holding the elevator door for someone else. The brief nod exchanged. Little polite rituals. The way thank yous and sorrys lubricate social life. The way sometimes we mumble them, sometimes we mean them intensely. Words perform social functions beyond content. I think of the first time someone said "I love you" to me and how those words hung, heavy, waiting for echo. That moment of risk again. Speaking is risky. Writing too. Especially writing honest things.

But maybe honesty isn't the aim here. Maybe it's play. So I'll play with sound: cellar door. Cellar door has been said to be one of the most beautiful phrases in English, not for meaning, but for phonetic quality. Say it aloud: cellar door. It rolls. It's a magic phrase. It opens into a dark cool place under the house, full of jars and dust and secrets. Now there's a memory: my grandmother's cellar, shelves of canned peaches, the smell of earth and sweet fruit. A bare bulb swinging. She sent me down to fetch pickles. I was afraid of spiders. I overcame fear for pickles.

This is what happens when you let someone write whatever comes: you get a jumble of images, an oscillation between concrete scenes and meta-commentary. You get me writing about writing. You get small stories that begin and end abruptly. You get musings on time, on memory, on clouds. Did I mention clouds? High cirrus streaking like brushstrokes, cumulus piling up like whipped cream, storm clouds bruised and full of energy. The sky is an ever-changing canvas. Sometimes I lie on grass and watch it, the drift calming. Maybe you do too. Maybe you haven't in a while.

At this point, I feel close to the arbitrary goal of 1000 words. There's a sense of rounding off. To end, perhaps return to the beginning: the bicyclist in the yellow jacket. Let's let him arrive somewhere. He turns down a side street, slows, pulls up to a house with a blue door (there it is again). He leans his bike against the porch. He takes off his red gloves, stuffs them in his pocket, and knocks. Inside, someone hears, footsteps approach. The door opens. A smile. "You're here," a voice says. "Yes," he says, catching his breath. He steps inside. Behind him, the dog that had chased him earlier wanders by, sniffs, decides not to bark. The door closes. The street is quiet again.

Words end. Silence fills.
